name: Hex
tagline: A collaborative workspace where SQL and Python notebooks turn into shareable interactive data apps.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core mechanic, cells that mix SQL against a warehouse with Python that reads the query results as dataframes, is not exotic: DuckDB plus a notebook kernel plus a chart library gets you most of the analysis loop in a weekend. What you cannot one-shot is the part Hex actually sells, which is the layer above the notebook: multiplayer editing, a published app view your non-technical coworkers can use without seeing code, scheduled runs, permissions, and connection management across Snowflake and BigQuery and Postgres. For a solo analyst poking at their own data, a local notebook is honestly fine and faster. For a team where the deliverable is a link someone else trusts, the DIY version falls over on day two. So: buildable, with the gaps sitting exactly where the money is.
coreLoopDIY: A local notebook where SQL cells run against DuckDB or your Postgres, Python cells read the results as dataframes, and a toggle hides the code to render just the charts and inputs as a shareable page.
requirements: DuckDB for local files, plus connection strings for any real database you want to query
Warehouse credentials in .env if you are hitting Snowflake or BigQuery
Comfort running a dev server whenever you want to open your own notebooks
whatYouLose: Real-time multiplayer editing and comment threads on cells
A published app view with access controls that non-technical people can open on their own
Scheduled runs, caching, and alerting when a query result changes
Maintained connectors and query pushdown for Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and friends
Version history, review flows, and the general confidence that a shared dashboard is not silently broken
moatNotes: The notebook is the commodity. The published-app-with-permissions layer and the warehouse connectors are the product.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the artifact that matters is not the notebook, it is the link. Hex exists so an analyst can hand a stakeholder something interactive that queries live data, refreshes on a schedule, respects row permissions, and does not require the stakeholder to know what a kernel is. Getting a self-hosted notebook to serve that reliably to a dozen people means auth, a scheduler, connection pooling, result caching, and somebody on call when the Snowflake credentials rotate. That is a job, not a weekend, and per-seat pricing is cheaper than the job.
notes: Personal data exploration is a solved local problem; the moment you need to share it with someone who does not write code, the weekend build stops being enough.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user hybrid SQL and Python notebook that can publish itself as a read-only data app.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, uvicorn.
- Execution: one long-lived Python process per notebook using a single shared globals dict. No Jupyter, no ipykernel.
- SQL engine: DuckDB in-process. It reads local CSV and Parquet files directly, and can ATTACH a Postgres database if POSTGRES_URL is set in .env.
- Frontend: React with Vite and TypeScript. CodeMirror 6 for the editors. Vega-Lite via react-vega for charts. Plain CSS, no UI framework.
- Storage: notebooks are .json files in ./notebooks/. No database, no accounts, no telemetry.

Data model: a notebook is an ordered list of cells. Cell types are sql, python, markdown, and input. Each cell has an id, a type, source text, an optional name, and a hideCode flag.

Behavior:
- SQL cells run against DuckDB. The result is registered back into the Python globals as a pandas DataFrame under the cell's name, and DuckDB can query any prior named DataFrame by that name. This round trip is the whole point, make it work.
- Python cells run in the shared globals and can reference any named SQL result. Capture stdout, exceptions with tracebacks, and the value of the last expression.
- If a Python cell's last expression is a Vega-Lite spec dict or a DataFrame, render it as a chart or a paged table rather than text.
- Input cells define a named widget: text, number, date, or select with a static option list. Their value lands in globals and is interpolated into SQL via a {{name}} placeholder using DuckDB prepared parameters, not string concatenation.
- Run a single cell, or run all cells top to bottom. Show per cell status: idle, running, error, and last run duration.
- App mode: a /app/:notebookId route that renders only markdown, inputs, charts and tables, hiding every cell marked hideCode, with a Refresh button that re-runs everything. It is served by the same local process, it is not published anywhere.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build: authentication, multiplayer or CRDTs, scheduled runs, Snowflake or BigQuery connectors, cloud deploy, sharing links, version history, package installation UI.

Deliver a README with setup steps, a .env.example containing POSTGRES_URL, one example notebook that loads a bundled sample CSV, filters it with an input cell, and renders one chart, plus pytest coverage of the SQL to DataFrame to SQL round trip and of parameter interpolation.
